title: CTEs Are Not Materialized
description: A CTE referenced several times is re-executed each time; materializing it into a #temp table computes it once. Why it matters: CTEs are a beloved readability tool, but this is a common, costly misconception -- knowing when SQL Server actually materializes (or doesn't) a CTE prevents accidental repeated work.
narrative:
## What This Lesson Is About

Imagine writing out a complicated math calculation once at the top of your notes, giving it a nice short name like "Result A," and then, later in your notes, writing "Result A" three separate times expecting each mention to just reuse the answer you already worked out. In real math notes, that works because you actually wrote the number down once. But imagine instead that every time you wrote "Result A," a very literal-minded assistant re-did the entire original calculation from scratch, every single time, rather than reusing the answer — you'd get the same correct result, but you'd have paid for the work three times over instead of once. This lesson is about exactly that surprising behavior with Common Table Expressions, or CTEs, in SQL Server.

**What this lesson's topic actually is.** A CTE (written with a `WITH SomeName AS (...)` clause at the top of a query) is a named, reusable-looking block of SQL that you can then reference multiple times later in the same query, purely for readability — it lets you give a name to a complex subquery instead of repeating the whole thing inline every time you need it. It looks, very strongly, like it should be computed once and then reused, similar to a variable in a programming language. This lesson is about the fact that, in SQL Server, that assumption is usually wrong.

**Why this happens in real databases.** CTEs are a genuinely beloved tool because they make complex queries dramatically more readable — breaking a tangled nested subquery into a clearly-named, logical building block is a real, legitimate win for maintainability. But that readability benefit has nothing to do with execution behavior, and the two get conflated extremely easily, because in many other contexts (programming languages, spreadsheet formulas), naming something and reusing the name usually does imply "computed once, reused after."

**How it happens mechanically inside SQL Server.** A CTE is not a temporary table and it is not automatically materialized (meaning: computed once and stored somewhere) anywhere by SQL Server. Instead, it behaves essentially like a macro, or a stand-in for its own definition: every place in the outer query that references the CTE by name gets substituted, at compile time, with the CTE's actual underlying query definition, as if you had pasted the whole subquery in by hand at each reference point. If a CTE is referenced three times in the outer query, the optimizer builds a plan that runs that CTE's entire underlying logic three separate times — as three independent instances of the same subquery, not one computed result being reused three times. If that CTE's own definition involves a nontrivial join, aggregation, or filter over a decent-sized table, running it three times means paying that same cost three times over, even though from a plain reading of the SQL, it very much looks like "Result A" should only need to be figured out once.

This becomes especially costly when a CTE is used recursively or is itself moderately expensive and referenced multiple times in different parts of a larger query — the total cost isn't the cost of the CTE's logic, it's that cost multiplied by however many times it's referenced, which can turn what looks like an elegant, DRY (don't-repeat-yourself) piece of SQL into something that repeats a decent chunk of expensive work behind the scenes, invisibly, purely because of how CTEs are implemented.

**Why this matters in production.** This is a common, costly misconception precisely because CTEs are so widely recommended for readability, and the mental model "I named it, so it's computed once" is such a natural (and, in most other programming contexts, correct) assumption to bring into SQL. The performance cost is also easy to miss during development, because a small, fast underlying query multiplied by three references still finishes fast enough that nobody notices; it's only once the underlying CTE logic itself becomes moderately expensive, or the table it touches grows large, that the repeated-execution cost becomes visible and painful. Looking at the execution plan is the way to catch this: the CTE's underlying subquery logic (its joins, scans, aggregations) will show up multiple separate times in the plan tree, once per reference, rather than once with the result being reused.

The fix demonstrated in this lesson is to force materialization explicitly, most commonly by computing the CTE's logic once into a real `#temp` table (or table variable), and then having the rest of the query reference that temp table instead of the CTE by name. A `#temp` table genuinely is computed once and stored (in tempdb), so every subsequent reference to it really is reusing the same already-computed data, turning three executions of the underlying logic back into just one — matching the mental model people naturally (if incorrectly) bring to CTEs in the first place.

**Try it yourself.** The scenario below references the same CTE three times in one query and shows you its underlying logic appearing three separate times in the execution plan, each one independently re-executed. After rewriting the query to compute the same logic once into a `#temp` table and referencing that instead, re-run it and compare plans: the repeated subquery logic collapses down to a single computation, with the temp table simply being read back three times afterward — dramatically cheaper once the CTE's underlying logic is itself nontrivial.

**Beyond this exact scenario.** Recursive CTEs (used for things like organizational hierarchies or bill-of-materials explosions) are a related but distinct case worth knowing about separately — they genuinely do need to be understood as an iterative, repeated process by design, rather than "not materialized" in the same accidental sense covered here. The specific trap in this lesson is about a *non-recursive* CTE referenced multiple times for pure readability, where the repetition is unintentional and avoidable, as opposed to a recursive CTE's repetition, which is the whole point of how it works and isn't something to try to eliminate.

One more practical detail: SQL Server's newer versions have introduced some limited automatic CTE inlining optimizations in specific cases, but the safe assumption to build habits around is still that a CTE is re-evaluated per reference unless you've explicitly verified otherwise in the actual execution plan for your version and scenario.

## Scenario
A report defines a Common Table Expression that aggregates every order per customer, then references it several times (to filter against the average and the maximum). A widespread myth says the CTE is computed once and reused — so this *feels* cheap.

## Why it's slow
In SQL Server a CTE is **not** materialized. The optimizer **inlines the CTE's definition at every reference**. If `CustTotals` appears three times, the underlying `GROUP BY` over `Orders` is executed **three times** — three full scans of the 200,000-row table. The logical reads on `Orders` scale with the number of references.

## What to look for
- `Orders` in `STATISTICS IO` with a **scan count greater than 1** and logical reads several times a single scan.
- The same aggregation subtree repeated in the plan, once per CTE reference.

## The concept
A CTE is syntactic — it names a subquery, it does not cache a result. When you reference an expensive intermediate result **more than once**, materialize it yourself into a **#temp table** (which *does* store rows and carries statistics). The aggregation runs a single time; every later reference reads the small temp table instead of re-scanning the base table.
startingQuery:
WITH CustTotals AS
(
    SELECT CustomerId, SUM(Total) AS Revenue
    FROM Orders
    GROUP BY CustomerId
)
SELECT ct.CustomerId, ct.Revenue
FROM CustTotals ct
WHERE ct.Revenue > (SELECT AVG(Revenue) FROM CustTotals)
  AND ct.Revenue < (SELECT MAX(Revenue) FROM CustTotals);
hints: Check STATISTICS IO for Orders — how many times was it scanned? Compare that to how many times the CTE is referenced.
The CTE is inlined at every reference, so the GROUP BY over Orders runs once per mention — the table is not cached.
Materialize the aggregate once: SELECT ... INTO #CustTotals FROM Orders GROUP BY CustomerId; then query #CustTotals.
